CHIEF COMPLAINT
Second opinion regarding right index finger injury.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Philip Gutierrez is a 50-year-old right-handed male presenting for a second opinion regarding his right index finger. He sustained a hyperextension injury to his right index finger during a motor vehicle accident in March 2026, when the car he was in as a passenger was rear-ended multiple times, causing him to brace himself and stretch his right index finger backward. He reports the finger has been painful and swollen since the accident, approximately three months ago. He cannot make a fist and reports pain severity ranging from tolerable to unbearable, particularly with driving. He has been receiving occupational therapy and had an MRI of the finger. He reports confusion regarding treatment recommendations, as he was told by his orthopedist that an injection would worsen the tear, then later told an injection was recommended, leading him to seek this second opinion. He is right-handed and works as an X-ray technician, making hand function critical for his work.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis. Reports persistent swelling and pain in right index finger. Reports numbness in the finger. Denies other systemic complaints.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
None reported other than the current injury.

MEDICATIONS
Blood pressure medication (name not specified).

ALLERGIES
Dexamethasone (causes tachycardia/heart racing).
Methylprednisolone (causes itching).

FAMILY HISTORY
Not documented.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Works as an X-ray technician. Right-handed. Currently able to drive.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Heart rate regular rate and rhythm, 2+ radial pulse bilaterally.
General: Pleasant, cooperative, healthy-appearing male, no acute distress.
Right hand: No swelling or bruising in the palm over the volar surface of the index finger. Normal creases. Slightly diminished creases over the PIP of the index finger compared to the middle finger. Index finger rests in 10-degree PIP-flexed position. Pain with PIP extension and flexion. Mild numbness noted. Full active and passive range of motion of DIP and PIP joints demonstrated. Patient able to make fist. Tenderness with MCP joint flexion. Collateral ligaments intact. Extensors intact.

RESULTS
Right hand X-rays (4 views) from today: No bony abnormalities. Joint congruency throughout all lesser digits on the right hand. No soft tissue shadows of concern. No arthritis.
MRI from 4/24/2026: Focal soft tissue swelling over the right index MCP joint. Partial-thickness tear of the right flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) tendon. Fluid consistent with tenosynovitis around the FDS and flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendons. Radial and ulnar collateral ligaments of the index MCP joint intact. MCP joint capsule intact. Extensor tendons intact.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Post-traumatic severe stenosing tenosynovitis of the right index finger with partial-thickness tear of the flexor digitorum superficialis tendon. Significant scar tissue and inflammation are blocking tendon excursion.

Plan:
1. Corticosteroid injection: Administered betamethasone 1 cc with lidocaine 0.5 cc via trigger finger injection technique. Patient had dramatic painful reaction to needle insertion on first attempt and hand was withdrawn. Second attempt was made with same medication. A small palmar vein was encountered with minimal bleeding, cleaned and bandaged. Patient reassured that no harm was done to the finger.
2. Pain management: Recommended icing this evening and ibuprofen.
3. Occupational therapy: Outpatient physical therapy once weekly for 6 weeks with the patient's current provider. Goal is full active and passive range of motion with no restrictions. Emphasis on aggressive finger movement and bending exercises.
4. Patient counseled that improvement should begin within 3-5 days, with continued improvement over the next couple of weeks. Advised that the injection will help with inflammation and pain, making therapy more tolerable, but patient must perform the active motion work.
5. Reassured that patient has intact extensors and collateral ligaments, so movement will not cause further damage.
6. May repeat steroid injection if needed.
7. Safe to continue driving.
